newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Pharmacia & Upjohn says profits fall 12 percent.
newsitem.headline: Pharmacia & Upjohn says profits fall 12 percent.

text.p: Pharmacia & Upjohn, the Swedish-U.S. pharmaceutical company, said Thursday that its profits fell by 12 percent in the latest quarter and it predicted weaker-than-expected earnings for next year.
While the earnings report was in line with expectations, the London-based company's prediction of lower 1997 earnings sent its stock falling in Sweden and the United States.

The company, which was formed in a $6.9 billion merger of Sweden's Pharmacia and Upjohn of Kalamazoo, Mich., in August 1995, said net income for the three months ended Sept. 30 fell to $204 million, 39 cents a share, from $231 million, or 44 cents a share.
Shares of Pharmacia & Upjohn tumbled by 13.5 Swedish crowns ($2.06) on the Stockholm Stock Exchange to close at 229.5 crown ($35.05) -- their lowest close in nearly a year.
Pharmacia & Upjohn lost $2.125 to $35.625 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was among the most heavily traded issues.
Initially, investors reacted positively when the company posted results in line with an earlier warning over negative currency effects.
However, the shares sold off after the company told analysts later in the day that next year's earnings were likely to fall below market forecasts of $2.35 a share.

"It's a matter of credibility," analyst Stephen Putnam from Keinwort Benson said. "Three weeks ago we were told one thing and now the company's changed its story. This was like another profit warning."
Spokesman Jan Isoz said the company's chief finance director, Bob Salisbury, told analysts the consensus earnings forecast for 1997 was too high.
"The average forecast is around $2.35 and he said that it could be around 10 cents too high," Isoz said.
This was expected to trigger another round of profit revisions similar to when the company released a surprise profit warning three weeks ago for the third quarter.
The company unnerved investors when it said the weaker yen, stronger Swedish crown and Italian lira could drag earnings per share down.
The company said its sales rose 2 percent to $1.7 billion, although they would have been 4 percent higher if it were not for currency effects.
